explain.say: In 1584 a miller called Menocchio told the Inquisition that the world began like cheese, and the angels appeared in it like worms. He was eventually executed around 1599. In 1976 Carlo Ginzburg turned his trial records into The Cheese and the Worms. Watch the board zoom in, from all of Europe down to one man's words.

explain.say: Look at the fourth and fifth levels: a village called Montereale and its miller. Menocchio had read a few books, perhaps a Bible in Italian and travel tales, and mixed them with old peasant ideas. Ginzburg asked: what did ordinary readers make of the new printed world? Why might a miller meet so many people?

explain.say: Now the last level, the trial records. Interrogators wrote down Menocchio's answers. That is a rare chance to hear a peasant voice, but filtered through his questioners. This is what microhistory does: a very small scale, read very closely, to answer large questions. Whose voice is shaping the record here?

explain.say: Other classics followed. Look at the map. Natalie Zemon Davis wrote The Return of Martin Guerre, 1983, about a sixteenth-century French village and a man who claimed another's identity. Robert Darnton's The Great Cat Massacre, 1984, decoded a strange joke by print workers in 1730s Paris.

See the comparison: microhistory looks at the normal exception, an unusual case that reveals what was normal around it. Critics ask how typical one case can be. Wonderful focus. Exam tip: always say what wider question a microhistory answers, not just its story.

faq.a: Microhistory studies a small unit, like one person, village or event, in great detail to answer big historical questions. It began with Italian historians such as Carlo Ginzburg and Giovanni Levi in the 1970s.

Menocchio, Domenico Scandella, was a miller in Friuli in north-east Italy. Tried by the Inquisition for heresy, he described an unusual view of creation, and was executed around 1599. Ginzburg's The Cheese and the Worms tells his story.
asks: What is The Cheese and the Worms about?

faq.q: Why are trial records useful to historians?
faq.a: They record the words of ordinary people who rarely wrote anything. But they were shaped by the questions, fears and language of interrogators, so historians read them against the grain.
asks: What can Inquisition records tell us?

faq.q: What is The Return of Martin Guerre about?
faq.a: Natalie Zemon Davis's 1983 book studies a sixteenth-century case in Artigat in southern France, where a man posed as the returned Martin Guerre for years. It reveals village life, marriage and identity.
asks: Who wrote The Return of Martin Guerre?

faq.a: The idea, from Italian microhistorians, that an exceptional case, such as an odd trial, can reveal the normal rules and assumptions of its society, because the record shows where those rules were tested.

facts: Carlo Ginzburg's The Cheese and the Worms was published in Italian in 1976.
Natalie Zemon Davis's The Return of Martin Guerre was published in 1983.
Robert Darnton's The Great Cat Massacre was published in 1984.

quiz.why: The records of Menocchio's trials preserved his answers to interrogators.

wrong.1: Menocchio left no diary; his words survive through the trials.
wrong.2: A census would not record his ideas.
